comparator.name: Literary and Cultural Analysis (Literary Studies)
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 full-time course guide shows 60 EC per year. It places one 6 EC programme elective in each upper year. This example uses the first two 6 EC choices that appear in both the guide and the regulations. Free electives remain open.
components: The first year also includes an uncredited academic literacy test and tutoring. Tutoring continues in the upper years.
Introduction to Literary and Cultural Analysis
Key Concepts in Contemporary Arts, Media and Culture
Cultural Memory in Literary and Visual Arts
Complete the Literary and Cultural Analysis first year before taking this course.
Requires at least 48 EC in a Humanities bachelor’s programme.
Practicing Cultural Analysis: From Object to Case Study
Aesthetics and Politics illustrates the restricted 6 EC choice. It studies aesthetics, identity and collective memory.
The guide allocates 18 EC of free electives in year two.
Philosophy of the Humanities (LCA and English)
Requires a positive binding study advice for a Humanities bachelor’s programme.
Thesis Workshop Literary and Cultural Analysis
Complete most core courses before taking the workshop. It prepares students to design and write the thesis.
Moving Images Across Media illustrates the second restricted 6 EC choice. It studies moving images and how they represent mobility, feeling and political agency.
The guide allocates 24 EC of free electives in year three. Free electives can include a minor, study abroad or a placement, subject to the programme rules.
Bachelor's Thesis Literary and Cultural Analysis
Earn at least 120 EC before starting work with a supervisor. Take the Thesis Workshop in preparation for the thesis.

core: Close analysis of literature, art and popular culture across text, image, film, media and everyday cultural objects
Literary and cultural theory, critical interpretation and the construction of meaning
Historical, social, political and philosophical contexts of culture, including identity, inequality and power
Qualitative humanities research, academic writing, case-study construction and independent thesis work
adjacent: Visual art, cultural memory, museums and material or spatial cultural artefacts
Literature, film, media, intertextuality and intermedial storytelling
Culture, identity, colonialism, gender, politics, inequality and power
Cultural criticism and public cultural intervention
questions: How is meaning produced through close reading of literature, images, art and popular culture?
How do cultural forms reflect and shape society, identity, inequality and political power?
How do literary and cultural forms travel across media, periods and social contexts?

selection.assessment: The first option combines literary, visual and historical criticism. The second focuses on culture and power through institutions, history and representation. The third focuses on how stories and arguments change across media. The distinct course groups support three coherent options.

alternatives.label: Literary, Artistic & Cultural Analysis
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum integrates literary close reading and theory with art history, film and media, cultural memory, philosophy, sociology and qualitative and historical research.
alternatives.concept: Interpret literature, artworks and cultural objects through close reading, visual analysis and historical research. Study how museums, heritage and media shape what people remember and value.
progression: Introductory literature, art history and film analysis precede advanced interpretation, museum studies and historical research. Sociology and qualitative methods support the study of cultural institutions.

alternatives.label: Culture, Identity & Power
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum studies culture through history, political thought, sociology, media, literature, heritage and social movements, with sustained attention to inequality, identity and power.
alternatives.concept: Study how colonialism, gender, race and political power shape cultural expression. Use history, sociology and political theory to interpret literature, media and heritage.
alternatives.distinctness: 12 courses (90 EC) differ from the first option in each direction. Political thought, comparative politics, gender history, empire and social movements make power and institutions the organising focus.
progression: Introductory history, sociology and political philosophy prepare for studies of empire, representation, social movements, institutions and conflict. Qualitative methods support research on identity and power.

alternatives.label: Literature, Film & Cultural Communication
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum forms a clear sequence in literature, film, media, rhetoric and creative communication, complemented by art history, archaeology, philosophy and qualitative research.
alternatives.concept: Study how stories change as they move between writing, film and performance. Develop skills in adaptation analysis, documentary, rhetoric and creative communication.
alternatives.distinctness: 5 courses (37.5 EC) differ from the first option in each direction. Rhetoric, persuasion and media are central here. The first option gives more attention to art history, museums and historical inquiry.
progression: Literary, film and rhetoric foundations precede adaptation, documentary and persuasive communication. Stylistics and qualitative methods support close interpretation and creative projects.

blocks: Both introduce close reading, literary interpretation and foundational concepts for analysing texts and culture.
Both analyse moving images and representation. UCR introduces film form and media history. UvA focuses on mobility and the affective and political force of images.
Both use close analysis to explain how form creates meaning. UCR concentrates on language and style. UvA works across texts, images and objects.
Both take a comparative global approach to literary traditions and their cultural meanings.
Both mobilise theory through focused cultural case studies; UCR centres race and ethnicity in media.
Both analyse narrative construction across media; UCR focuses specifically on adaptation from text to film.

Both use literary and cultural theories to interpret texts. UCR applies perspectives such as Marxism, feminism and psychoanalysis to literary meaning. UvA covers a wider range of contemporary critical approaches.
Both examine relations among culture, media, technology and environmental or material questions.
Both engage advanced contemporary theory and debate; UCR approaches these debates through social theory and civil society.
Both provide philosophical foundations for humanities interpretation; UCR surveys historical philosophical traditions rather than philosophy of the humanities as a field.

notes.text: UCR offers related study in literary interpretation, visual culture, politics and media. UvA provides a sustained sequence in literary and cultural theory, case-study methods, thesis preparation and an independent 12 EC thesis.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

audience.programmeDescription: Literary Studies at the University of Amsterdam examines how texts, images and other cultural objects create meaning. Students develop methods in close reading, cultural theory and research before writing an independent thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers related options in literary and visual culture, culture and power, or literature and screen media. UvA devotes more of the degree to literary and cultural theory, analysis of cultural objects and thesis research.
